questions.q: List three specific incidents from "Vitamin-M" where Grandpa's memory loss is shown directly through his actions or speech.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Grandpa calling Ravi by his father's name, (2) Grandpa insisting he hasn't eaten when he just finished a meal, (3) Grandpa searching for his spectacles while wearing them. A wrong answer that lists only vague descriptions like "he forgets things" reveals the student cannot locate textual evidence -- a critical board-exam skill where specific references earn marks.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the incident of Grandpa's missing spectacles (which are on his head) functions differently in the story than the incident where he forgets Ravi's name.
questions.a: Correct answer: The spectacles incident uses gentle humour to show harmless absent-mindedness, inviting affectionate laughter; the name-forgetting incident carries emotional weight because it signals erasure of relationship, causing Ravi pain. A wrong answer that treats both as "just forgetfulness" reveals the student misses the author's intentional gradation from light to heavy moments -- a board-level analytical distinction.

questions.q: In the scene where Vidya serves Grandpa a second helping because he claims he hasn't eaten, identify the literary technique used to show her shift from irritation to care, and explain why this technique matters for the theme.
questions.a: Correct answer: The technique is "show, don't tell" through action -- Vidya doesn't argue or correct; she simply serves. This matters because it demonstrates the theme's core message: caring for memory loss requires adapting behavior, not correcting the patient. A wrong answer identifying "dialogue" or "description" reveals the student cannot distinguish narrative techniques -- a skill tested in 5-mark board questions.

questions.q: Compare how Grandpa's memory loss affects his relationship with Ravi versus his relationship with Vidya. Use two pieces of evidence for each relationship.
questions.a: Correct answer: With Ravi: (1) Name-forgetting creates distance, (2) Repeated stories become bonding moments when Ravi listens patiently. With Vidya: (1) Forgotten meals trigger her practical caregiving, (2) His dependence allows her to express love through service. A wrong answer that generalizes "both love him" reveals inability to differentiate character dynamics -- a comparative analysis skill required for 8-mark board questions.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the story's ending (Grandpa smiling at the vitamin bottle) resolves the theme of memory loss tragically or redemptively. Justify with two textual clues.
questions.a: Correct answer: Redemptively. Clue 1: Grandpa's smile shows retained emotional capacity despite cognitive loss. Clue 2: The vitamin bottle -- originally a symbol of medical intervention -- becomes a shared ritual of connection. A wrong answer calling it "sad because he still has memory loss" reveals the student equates theme resolution with problem-solving rather than emotional acceptance -- a sophisticated distinction examiners reward.

questions.q: Write a 50-word paragraph from Grandpa's perspective describing what it feels like when a memory "slips away," using one metaphor from the story and one original sensory detail.
questions.a: Good answer criteria: Uses the story's "fog" or "slipping sand" metaphor; adds original sensory detail (e.g., "cold tea on my tongue," "the rough edge of a familiar photograph"); maintains Grandpa's voice (simple, present-tense). A poor answer that writes in third person or uses only abstract nouns reveals the student cannot inhabit character perspective -- a creative writing skill often tested in 10-mark board tasks.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The theme of memory loss and aging explores how progressive cognitive decline affects an elderly person's identity, autonomy, and relationships, while ______ revealing the family's emotional journey from frustration to compassionate understanding.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your grandmother forgets she already added sugar to her tea and adds it three times -- you might feel annoyed at first, then sad, then ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can trace the theme of memory loss across at least three distinct episodes in the story, explain how each episode deepens the portrayal of aging, and articulate the author's message about dignity in cognitive decline using textual evidence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine your ______ forgets she already added sugar to her tea and adds it three times -- you might feel annoyed at first, then sad, then protective.
